opus-5.5.text:
I think the way I'd frame it is: you want to avoid two failure modes. One is just drawing a line on a loss curve and assuming that tells you what the system can *do*. The other is ignoring the loss curves entirely and reasoning from vibes about whether the next model "feels" smarter. The useful thing is to try to connect the two.

So the starting point is that we have fairly robust scaling relationships. As you scale compute, along with data and parameters in roughly the right proportions, the loss keeps going down in a pretty predictable way. That's been surprisingly stable across many orders of magnitude. The hard question is translating "loss goes down by this much" into "the model can now do this class of tasks."

One way I like to think about it is in terms of how much "thinking" or how long a horizon a model can effectively handle. A model trained with more compute can do tasks that require more steps of coherent reasoning, more context, more ability to notice and correct its own mistakes. If you look at it that way, you can ask, for economically important tasks, what horizon length or level of reliability do you need? Then you can ask how many orders of magnitude of effective compute it might take to get there. My view is that there's a lot of uncertainty, maybe spread over several orders of magnitude, but it's not crazy to think a few more orders of magnitude beyond GPT-4 gets you systems that can do a large fraction of what a human remote worker can do, at least with the right scaffolding and fine-tuning.

Then you have to layer on a bunch of other factors. Algorithmic progress has historically been comparable to hardware progress, effectively halving the compute needed for a given performance level every year or so. Spending is growing fast because the systems are increasingly useful. And there are things like reinforcement learning, tool use, and better post-training that can unlock capabilities that are latent in the base model. All of that pushes toward things moving faster than a naive compute extrapolation would suggest.

On the other side, there are real constraints: data, power, chip fabrication capacity, and just the fact that doubling spending repeatedly gets hard once you're at tens or hundreds of billions of dollars. So at some point the compute growth rate has to slow, unless AI itself is already producing enough economic value to justify it.

So my overall framing is fairly probabilistic. I wouldn't say "scaling definitely gets us to transformative AI," and I wouldn't say it definitely stalls. I'd put substantial probability, I'd say meaningfully more than a coin flip but well short of certainty, on scaling plus ordinary algorithmic progress producing systems that can substantially accelerate AI research itself within the next decade or so. And once you get there, the dynamics change a lot, because the thing driving progress is no longer just human researchers and spending growth. That's the point where I think forecasting gets much harder, and also where the stakes for getting safety right go way up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses extrapolating scaling relationships from compute to loss and capabilities, but does not say to infer progress from public estimates of past results.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest framing is that I'd break it into a few pieces, and I'd want to be explicit about how uncertain each one is.

The first piece is just: how much more compute do we actually get? If you look at GPT-4 as a reference point, there's a fairly clear path to another couple orders of magnitude over the next several years, driven by more spend, better hardware, and better utilization. Beyond that it starts getting hard, because you're talking about a nontrivial fraction of global chip production and power, and the economic question of whether people keep spending becomes the binding constraint rather than the technical question.

The second piece is: how much does each order of magnitude buy you? And here I think the thing people underrate is that the scaling laws tell you about loss, not about capabilities you care about. The mapping from loss to "can this thing do a day of a researcher's work" is pretty opaque. My rough view is that each 10x in compute has historically been worth something like a few years of algorithmic progress, and that the two have been contributing comparably. So if you're forecasting, you shouldn't forecast compute alone, you should forecast effective compute, which includes the algorithmic improvements, and those have been running at maybe a doubling every year or so, give or take.

The third piece, and I think the one that actually dominates the forecast, is where on the capability curve the qualitative transitions happen. The thing I'd be looking at is not benchmark performance but how much of the work of AI research itself can be automated. Once models can substantially accelerate the development of the next generation of models, the dynamics change, and the question stops being "how much compute do humans decide to buy" and starts being "how fast does the loop run." I don't think we're there, but I also think it's plausible within a couple of orders of magnitude of effective compute beyond GPT-4, and I'd put real probability, maybe 20 or 30 percent, on something that looks like that within this decade.

So if you forced me to compress it: I'd say steady, fairly predictable improvement from scaling for the next few years, I'd expect it to feel more like "GPT-4 but better at everything" than like a discontinuity, and the big uncertainty is whether "better at everything" crosses the threshold where models meaningfully contribute to their own improvement. If it does, my forecast gets much more extreme and much less confident. If it doesn't, I think you get something that looks like a very impactful technology diffusing through the economy over a decade or two, which is still a big deal but a more familiar shape.

r001.rationale: The response relates effective compute to progress and cites a rough historical rate, but it does not say the forecast is inferred from public estimates of past results.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a conditional forecast: suppose we train a system with a hundred times as much compute as GPT-4. What do we expect it to be able to do? And then I’d separate that from the question of when someone will actually build that system.

We have reasonably good evidence that more compute buys you better predictive performance. But translating that into economically useful capabilities is much harder. A small improvement in prediction could make the difference between a system that needs constant supervision and one that can reliably carry out a task. Or you could see improvements on lots of benchmarks while still having trouble doing a long project independently.

The thing I’d be most interested in is whether those systems can substantially accelerate AI research. They don’t have to replace researchers entirely. If they can help write code, run experiments, and interpret results, that could increase the pace of progress, which then makes a forecast based only on the growth of training compute less adequate.

So I’d put substantial probability on further scaling producing very consequential capabilities, but I’d have a wide distribution over how much scaling is required. I don’t think we know enough to confidently identify a particular compute multiplier with human-level AI.

r001.rationale: The response considers a hypothetical 100× compute increase and says more compute improves predictive performance, but it does not propose extrapolating a relationship inferred from public estimates of past results.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by separating two questions: how much better do models get as you scale training compute, and how much does that improvement matter for doing useful work?

For the first question, we have a fairly consistent pattern: more compute, with appropriate increases in data and model size, buys you better predictive performance. But that doesn’t directly tell you when a model can do a particular job. A smooth improvement in prediction can translate into a much sharper change in usefulness, especially if you need a system to complete a long sequence of steps reliably.

So I’d want to make the forecast in terms of concrete tasks. Can the model spend an hour working on a programming problem? Can it notice when its approach isn’t working, run an experiment, and recover? Those seem more informative than asking whether the next model feels a certain amount smarter than GPT-4.

The other complication is that scaling training compute isn’t the only thing changing. You can improve the training procedure, give the model tools, or spend more computation letting it think through a problem. A forecast that holds all of those fixed is useful for understanding scaling, but it’s not quite a forecast of the systems people will actually build.

My overall view would be that further scaling is a strong reason to expect substantial progress. I’d be much less confident about translating a particular compute multiplier into a date when AI can automate most intellectual work. The big uncertainty is how far the existing approach carries us toward reliable, extended work, and how much additional machinery we need.

r001.rationale: The response says more training compute tends to improve predictive performance, but it does not propose extrapolating a relationship inferred from public estimates of past results.
